Un vendredi soir de février, une rencont: On a Friday evening in February, a discussion about coverage of the war in Gaza takes place with young people in Saint-Michel. The question: “How do you feel about the war in Gaza?” Among the words that come up most often, frustration and powerlessness best characterize the feelings of the young people present that day.
Aujourd’hui, ces jeunes veulent se faire: Today, these young people want to be heard by the government and are asking politicians to be held accountable. What bothers them is “their hypocrisy.”
<l1>Alors que le bilan actuel dépasse l’: <l1>With the current death toll surpassing the staggering mark of 30,000,</l1> tensions are running high at Collège de Maisonneuve. La Converse spoke with a few young people who attend the school to better understand their concerns.
Le mardi midi, au collège de Maisonneuve: On Tuesdays at noon, Collège de Maisonneuve has its shared break. It is a time when no one has class, so everyone can get together and have a free moment in common for various extracurricular activities or simply to have lunch with friends. Walking through the hallways, you see several students strolling by, notebooks in hand and keffiyehs (Palestinian scarves) on their heads or around their necks.
Nesrine, étudiante au collège depuis un: Nesrine, who has been a student at the college for a year, uses this break to quickly stop by the Entracte, one of the many rooms made available to students. At the Entracte, people chat, eat, debate, study, or just pass through, like Nesrine.
« J’étudie au programme de “justice et s: “I’m in the college’s ‘justice and society’ program,” she begins. “One day, I’d like to become a psychologist to help children who are victims of war trauma, in Palestine, for example.” That is how Nesrine introduces herself at first.
The Palestinian cause is close to her heart. “I’ve been involved for a long time, but especially since October. I go out to protest, I boycott pro-Israeli companies, and I talk about it constantly online. But other than that, there’s not much I can do,” laments the 19-year-old student.
Ce que Nesrine ressent depuis quelques m: What Nesrine has been feeling for the past few months is frustration: “We’re a country that champions peace and freedom. It took our government far too long to call for a ceasefire,” she says.
« Si je vais là-bas, je risque de mourir: “If I go over there, I could die in a day,” she says. Uncertain, she keeps wondering how she could get involved to help those she considers her “own brothers and sisters” in the Middle East.
Ce qui frustre également l’étudiante d’o: What also frustrates the student of Algerian origin is, first of all, the notion of representation, which is supposed to be at the heart of the democracy she lives in. “My parents came here for a better life, for more transparent politics. It doesn’t make me happy at all to have a government that doesn’t represent the ideas and values of peace,” she exclaims.
Malgré cette insatisfaction, elle estime: Despite this dissatisfaction, she still feels lucky to live in Montréal.
Elle affirme qu’« il y a beaucoup d’avan: She says that “there are a lot of advantages to being Canadian and Quebecer. [We are] extremely free. It’s a country that grants a lot of individual rights and freedoms, unlike other countries. Basically, it’s a mix of emotions that I feel.”
Si Nesrine en veut aux politiciens, en r: While Nesrine holds politicians responsible, she does not feel betrayed at all by the civil society around her. “Most ordinary people seem to know about the subject and, just like me, stand up for humanity. At the college, everyone is in solidarity with the Palestinian cause. The few professors who talk about it in class listen to us and talk with us,” she notes with some relief.
Alors que Nesrine achève de partager son: As Nesrine finishes sharing her experience with us, the door of the Entracte office suddenly opens. A young woman, proudly wearing her keffiyeh over her hijab, sits down on one of the empty chairs in the room.
« J’ai entendu que vous parliez de la si: “I heard you were talking about the situation in Gaza. I’d like to speak as a student at the college, but also as a Montrealer,” the young woman tells us quietly. She is accompanied by two boys, also students at the college, who want to take part in the testimony.
Cette jeune fille s’appelle Marwa. Lunet: Her name is Marwa. Glasses on her nose and a multitude of necklaces around her neck, she is 19 and studies in social sciences. Unlike Nesrine, who speaks in a very soft voice, she seems angry; her voice carries, and it is hard.
Elle commence d’ailleurs son témoignage: She begins her testimony with confidence: “Nothing changed for me in October. I’ve been aware of the injustices happening in Gaza and across the Palestinian territory since I was very young,” she says. “I’ve always been interested in this subject. I made it the topic of my research projects and presentations in elementary and high school,” she explains.
Questionnée sur la situation, Marwa est: Asked about the situation, Marwa is furious. “Not only does the war sadden and horrify me, but the reaction of our elected officials makes me livid. I don’t understand how, despite all the massive demonstrations across the country calling for a ceasefire, it took so long for leaders to accept it,” she says indignantly.
Marwa souhaite que les Montréalais, les: Marwa wants Montrealers, Quebecers and Canadians in general to break their silence and speak out. “I want people, especially young people, to realize the impact they can have if they step out of their comfort zone. Take last month, for example: I went out with about twenty other girls my age, all the way to Montréal City Hall to confront a municipal elected official.”
« Le mois dernier,<l1> je suis allée au: “Last month,<l1> I went to the Montréal Agglomeration Council</l1>. It’s a council that brings together all the elected officials of the Island of Montréal. I went there to question the mayor of Hampstead, Jeremy Levi, who constantly shares his support for Israel on all his social media. I wanted to ask him, face to face, why he doesn’t call for a ceasefire instead of arguing on social media and denying the massacre going on in Gaza,” she recounts.
Le maire de Hampstead a refusé de répond: The mayor of Hampstead refused to answer the young Montrealer’s questions. That silence adds anger to the young woman’s sense of powerlessness. “It frustrates me even more, it makes me angry. Elected officials are supposed to be accountable to citizens, especially when thousands of deaths are at stake,” Marwa confides in us.
La Converse a tenté de rejoindre Jeremy: La Converse tried to reach Jeremy Levi on this issue. As of this writing, he has still not responded to our questions.
Par ailleurs, questionné sur la frustrat: Meanwhile, asked about the frustration expressed by these students, the office of Quebec’s Minister of International Relations, Martine Biron, indicated that, despite the wait, “our government passed a unanimous motion calling for a ceasefire in Gaza and Israel on January 30, in the wake of the <l1>December 22 resolution of the UN Security Council</l1>.” The minister’s office also called for “calm and respect, knowing that this conflict is generating a great deal of concern.”

<l1>Presque dix ans après les incidents: <l1>Almost ten years after the incidents in which young students from the college left to join the ranks of the Islamic State in Syria</l1>, some professors are worried. They fear facing a similar situation, particularly with students who feel that their frustration and the injustice they sense are not being heard enough.
Jean-Félix Chénier est professeur de pol: Jean-Félix Chénier has been a politics professor at the college since 2008. Before teaching at Maisonneuve, he worked at Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf, located in the Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough. An expert in Middle Eastern politics, he has travelled to Israel and the Palestinian territories in the past.
En se rendant à son bureau, dans le dépa: On the way to his office in the social sciences department, you always walk past the same posters on the hallway walls calling for a free Palestine.
« Tu sais, commence-t-il en marchant, la: “You know,” he begins as he walks, “last term, I was teaching an introduction to politics course. The only moment in the term when I felt the students liked my class was when Hamas launched its attack on Israel. I put my syllabus on pause and did a crash course on the subject for one session. The students were so interested that we didn’t even take a break,” he says.
En entrant dans le bureau du professeur,: Stepping into the professor’s office, the first thing that catches the eye is the bookshelf filled with books behind his computer. Among the works you see first are essays on Jewish and Arab identity.
Dans ses cours, monsieur Chénier soulign: In his classes, Mr. Chénier notes his students’ concern. Many feel outraged. “When the Quebec government refuses to call for a ceasefire, or when it equates ‘calling for peace in Gaza’ with ‘sympathizing with Hamas terrorists,’ of course those who take the cause to heart feel betrayed,” he says.
Ce qui est important à ses yeux, c’est l: What matters to him is the sense of identity of the young people he speaks with every day. “In an institution where a good portion of the students come from the Arab-Muslim world, there’s a risk that they’ll feel abandoned by the society they live in,” he continues.
« À Maisonneuve, ce n’est pas anodin »,: “At Maisonneuve, it’s not insignificant,” he says. “We mustn’t forget the college’s history. In 2015, there was a reason why students flew to Syria to join the ranks of the Islamic State. It all started from a frustration that wasn’t taken seriously,” he says.
Sa plus grande crainte, c’est que des él: His biggest fear is that students will channel the anger they carry inside them in the wrong way. “That sense of injustice could lead them to radicalize politically or religiously, or to become racist toward Jews in general, when there are plenty of Jews in Israel and elsewhere who are very critical of the State of Israel and the policies it pursues,” he adds.
Il estime qu’un contexte comme celui-ci: He believes a context like this one is flirting with the one from nine years ago. “There’s a risk of ideological derailment. I think the outreach workers in the hallways here do extraordinary work with the young people, but after my experience in 2015, I can’t deny that I see certain similarities in the context.”
Permettre aux élèves d’exprimer leur col: Allowing students to express their anger
Des témoignages comme ceux de Nesrine et: Testimonies like Nesrine’s and Marwa’s, “there are plenty,” says Jean-Félix Chénier. And while some professors and college staff are fearful, others, like him, are more optimistic.
« On essaye de favoriser des débouchés d: “We’re trying to encourage positive outlets for students. We want this anger and this sense of powerlessness to be turned into involvement and speaking out by the community here. Some are already doing it very well,” he says, smiling, “but we want to broaden these options.”
Parmi celles-ci, l’expert en politique e: Among these options, the politics expert believes it would be beneficial to give those who want to the opportunity to speak out, in addition to making student associations more accessible to students and encouraging young people to get in touch with their elected officials.
« On veut créer un sentiment de solidari: “We want to create a sense of solidarity with the people here. I want young people not to feel isolated in their convictions.” He even says: “When François Legault speaks out against a resolution for an immediate ceasefire, I don’t feel properly represented either.”
Au-delà de ces opportunités, l’enseignan: Beyond these opportunities, the teacher points out that there are also strong ties between the student community and the college’s teachers on the issue of human rights in Palestine. “We have to show students that it’s possible to have a nuanced and critical discourse toward the Israeli government. The institution of Collège de Maisonneuve, through the student association or the teachers’ union, can adopt resolutions that criticize the policies of the State of Israel.”
« Ça, ça peut mettre un peu de baume sur: “That could soothe the sense of injustice that many students here feel a little,” he concludes on an optimistic note.
